The unanswered question is whether ICE’s 287(g) expansion is worth its social and financial costs. Earlier research found harm to community trust without measurable reductions in crime.

As ICE’s 287(g) program expands, some states are moving the other direction. New Mexico, Maine, and Maryland banned the program in 2025–2026, joining six other states that already prohibited participation.

The expansion of ICE’s 287(g) program is not confined to border states. While Florida and Texas dominate the numbers, the program now spans rural counties, mid-size cities, and major metros across the country.

According to a February 2026 FWD.us analysis, the expansion of ICE’s 287(g) program could send $1.4B–$2B to local law enforcement this year, potentially the largest federal infusion into policing since the 1990s.

Most of the expansion in ICE’s 287(g) program comes from the Task Force Model: 1,188 agreements and counting. This model allows local officers to make immigration arrests on the street, not just inside jails.
ICE’s 287(g) program has expanded dramatically since January 2025. Active agreements with local law enforcement grew from 135 to 1,870 in just 16 months, spanning 39 states and 2 U.S. territories.

The numbers alone can’t answer the central question: Is the decline in asylum grants about changing applicant profiles, or pressure on immigration judges? The implications for due process are enormous.

Immigration judges completed 81,932 cases in March 2026 alone. Of those, 57,874 ended in removal orders and another 9,075 in voluntary departure orders. This is part of an FY2026 trend where 80% of completed cases end in deportation.
In February 2026, just 33.3% of immigrants had legal representation when removal orders were issued. Most people facing deportation are going through high-stakes legal proceedings without a lawyer.

A 2026 investigation by NYT reported that the immigration judges fired since January 2025 disproportionately had three things in common: Democratic appointments, experience representing immigrants, and above-average asylum grant rates.

After peaking at 3.4 million cases in December 2025, the immigration court backlog has declined modestly. Courts are completing cases at 1.65 times the pace of new filings, even after more than 100 immigration judges were fired since January 2025.
So far in FY2026, immigration courts granted asylum in under 10% of cases, the lowest rate ever recorded. Meanwhile, the same court system is carrying a backlog of 3.3 million pending cases.

More on my Substack. austinkocher.substack.com

CNN investigation on understaffing and deaths (May 15, 2026): cnn.com/2026/05/15/us/ice-im…

A key limitation: ICE has not released all required death reports, and cause of death is still undetermined in many recent cases The actual toll is likely higher than what's officially documented.

This happened as key detention oversight bodies (CRCL, the USCIS Ombudsman, and the Immigration Detention Ombudsman) were gutted or shuttered, and then only partially reopened with contractor staffing.

It is often treated as a simple function of current population versus stated capacity. Its etymology is weird: it leaves the term “crowding” un-interrogated as a root concept. I think it gets overused because it works so well in news headlines.

The treatment of detained people is a real problem and part of the problem comes down to the number of people inside of ICE facilities. But I have never liked this term “overcrowding.” It has no legal or analytical definition.
